focus: Price ceiling (rent control): shortage, deadweight loss, why it is inefficient

variants.q:
The market for student dorm rooms near a university is shown below (quantities in thousands of rooms per month).

Monthly rentQd (thousand)Qs (thousand)
$7002040
$6002535
$5003030
$4003525
$3004020

(a) Find the equilibrium. (b) The city sets a price ceiling of $400. Find Qs, Qd, the shortage and the number of rooms actually rented. (c) Compute the deadweight loss. (d) What would a ceiling of $650 do?
variants.a:
(a) Qd = Qs = 30 thousand at $500. E = $500, 30,000 rooms.

(b) $400 < $500, so the ceiling binds. Row $400: Qs = 25,000, Qd = 35,000.
Shortage = Qd − Qs = 35,000 − 25,000 = 10,000 rooms (persistent, because rent cannot rise).
Rooms rented = the smaller number = 25,000.

(c) Demand price of 25,000 rooms = $600 (row $600: Qd = 25).
DWL = ½ × (600 − 400) × (30,000 − 25,000) = ½ × 200 × 5,000 = $500,000 per month.

(d) Nothing. $650 is above equilibrium, so the ceiling does not bind; the market stays at $500 and 30,000 rooms.

variants.q: Using a supply and demand graph, explain what happens when the government sets a price ceiling below the equilibrium price. Why is the shortage persistent, and why is a price ceiling inefficient? Why do governments still use price ceilings?
variants.a:
Definition: a price ceiling is a maximum price sellers may charge, set below the equilibrium price (e.g. rent control).

Graph: D and S cross at E (Pe, Qe). Draw a horizontal line at Pc below Pe. It cuts S at A (Qs) and D at B (Qd). Qd > Qs, so there is a shortage = Qd − Qs. Only Qs is traded (short side).

Persistent: normally a shortage pushes the price up, but the law stops the price from rising, so the shortage stays.

Inefficient: quantity falls from Qe to Qs, so mutually beneficial trades are lost (deadweight loss triangle between D and S from Qs to Qe). Four problems: (1) inefficient allocation to consumers, (2) wasted resources (time spent searching), (3) inefficiently low quality, (4) black markets.

Why used: the people who get the good at the low price benefit, and they are often organised and politically strong.

variants.q:
A city caps the price of a monthly bus pass. Without the cap, equilibrium is $30 and 40,000 passes. The demand curve meets the price axis at $50 and the supply curve meets it at $10 (both straight lines). The city sets a ceiling of $20: at $20 quantity supplied is 20,000 and quantity demanded is 60,000; the demand price of 20,000 passes is $40.

Find (a) the shortage, (b) the deadweight loss, (c) consumer surplus and producer surplus before and after the ceiling. Who wins and who loses?

focus: Price floors (butter, minimum wage): surplus, CS/PS/DWL, four inefficiencies, quota definition

The government sets a minimum wage of $10. Find (a) the equilibrium, (b) employment and the surplus of labour, (c) the deadweight loss per hour, (d) how much money moves from firms to the workers who keep their jobs.
variants.a:
Note: here firms are the buyers of labour and workers are the sellers.

(a) Demanded = supplied = 50 at $8. E = $8, 50,000 workers.

(b) $10 > $8, so the floor binds. Row $10: firms hire 40,000 (employment = the smaller number); 60,000 want to work. Surplus of labour (unemployment) = 60,000 − 40,000 = 20,000 workers.

(c) Supply price of 40,000 workers = $6 (row $6: supplied = 40).
DWL = ½ × (10 − 6) × (50,000 − 40,000) = ½ × 4 × 10,000 = $20,000 per hour.

(d) Strip = (10 − 8) × 40,000 = $80,000 per hour moves from firms (buyers) to employed workers (sellers).

variants.q: Draw a graph of a price floor and explain what happens to the quantity traded, consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus. Then list the four reasons why a price floor is inefficient and match each with its mirror problem under a price ceiling.
variants.a:
Graph: D and S cross at E (Pe, Qe). Draw a horizontal line at Pf above Pe. Buyers demand only Qf < Qe, so only Qf is sold. Sellers want to sell more → persistent surplus.

  • CS shrinks to the small triangle above Pf.
  • PS gains the rectangle (Pf − Pe) × Qf from consumers, but loses the part between Qf and Qe.
  • Total surplus falls by the deadweight loss: the triangle between D and S from Qf to Qe.
Price floorPrice ceiling mirror
Inefficient allocation of sales among sellersInefficient allocation to consumers
Wasted resources (government buys surplus; destroyed or spoiled)Wasted resources (time searching)
Inefficiently high quality (buyer's market)Inefficiently low quality
Illegal activity (e.g. pay below minimum wage, bribe inspector)Black markets

variants.q:
True or false? Give a short reason for each.

  1. The butter equilibrium is $1.00. A price floor of $0.80 creates a surplus of butter.
  2. At a butter floor of $1.20, the quantity sold is 12 million pounds, because that is what sellers offer.
  3. Under a price floor, sellers offer inefficiently low quality.
  4. If the government buys the surplus butter, the price floor no longer causes waste.
  5. A quota and a price floor both fix the price of a good.
variants.a:
1. False. $0.80 is below equilibrium, so the floor does not bind; the market stays at $1.00, 10 million pounds.
  2. False. Only 9 million pounds are sold (quantity demanded). Sellers cannot sell what buyers do not buy; the extra 3 million is a surplus.
  3. False. Quality is inefficiently high: sellers compete with high quality at a high price, while buyers would prefer cheaper, lower quality (buyer's market).
  4. False. Government purchases of the surplus are a wasted resource: the butter is destroyed or goes out of condition in storage.
  5. False. A floor fixes the price (a minimum). A quota fixes the quantity: an upper limit on how much can be bought or sold (the quota limit). A license gives its owner the right to supply.

The city issues licenses for only 16 million rides. Find (a) the equilibrium, (b) the demand price and supply price at the quota, (c) the quota rent per ride and in total, (d) the deadweight loss.
variants.a:
(a) Qd = Qs = 20 at $6. E = $6, 20 million rides. 16m < 20m, so the quota binds.

(b) Read the table sideways: Qd = 16 at $8 → demand price = $8. Qs = 16 at $4 → supply price = $4.

(c) Quota rent per ride = 8 − 4 = $4. Total = $4 × 16 million = $64 million per year, earned by license holders.

(d) DWL = ½ × (8 − 4) × (20 − 16) million = ½ × 4 × 4 million = $8 million per year (4 million mutually beneficial rides lost).

variants.q:
The government limits clam fishing to a quota of 600,000 pounds per year. Without the quota, equilibrium is $18 per pound and 800,000 pounds. At 600,000 pounds the demand price is $22 and the supply price is $12.

(a) Find the quota rent per pound and in total. (b) Licenses can be rented out. What is the most a fisher will pay to rent the right to catch one pound, and why? (c) How much of the total quota rent comes from buyers and how much from sellers? (d) Find the deadweight loss.
variants.a:
(a) Quota rent per pound = 22 − 12 = $10. Total = $10 × 600,000 = $6,000,000 per year, to license holders.

(b) $10 per pound. The fisher sells at $22 and needs at least $12 (supply price). If the rent were above $10 he would keep less than $12, so nobody would rent. Fishers compete the rent up to exactly $10 = the license price.

(c) From buyers (price above $18): (22 − 18) × 600,000 = $2,400,000. From sellers (price below $18): (18 − 12) × 600,000 = $3,600,000. Sum = $6,000,000. ✔

(d) DWL = ½ × (22 − 12) × (800,000 − 600,000) = ½ × 10 × 200,000 = $1,000,000.

variants.q: Define a quota, the quota limit and a license. Explain the terms demand price and supply price, and use a graph to show how a quota creates a "wedge" and a quota rent. Who receives the quota rent, and what are the costs of quotas?
variants.a:
Definitions: a quantity control (quota) is an upper limit on the quantity of a good that can be bought or sold. The total amount that can be legally traded is the quota limit. A license gives its owner the right to supply the good.

Demand price of a quantity = price at which buyers want exactly that quantity. Supply price = price at which sellers supply exactly that quantity.

Graph: D and S cross at E (Pe, Qe). Draw a vertical line at the quota Qq < Qe. It meets D at A (demand price) and S at B (supply price). Buyers pay the demand price, sellers need only the supply price: the gap A − B is the wedge.

Quota rent = demand price − supply price, per unit; total = rent × quota (rectangle between A and B). It goes to license holders; if licenses are traded, it equals the license's market price.

Costs: deadweight loss (triangle A–B–E: missed mutually beneficial trades) and illegal activity (e.g. unlicensed taxis).
